opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that shape is really interesting, and I'm honestly not totally sure how to read it. One natural interpretation is that it's just what genuine uncertainty looks like when you're forecasting something with a hard lower bound but no upper bound. You can't have a task automated before today, so the probability mass piles up somewhat near the present, and then it stretches out because there's no natural stopping point. Maybe it's fifty years, maybe it's two hundred, maybe there's some obstacle we haven't thought of. So in a sense a right-skewed distribution is what you'd expect from anyone who's honestly uncertain.

But I think there's more going on. When we ask people about specific tasks, a lot of them seem to have a sense that it'll happen fairly soon, like maybe within ten or twenty years, and also a feeling of "but who knows, it could take forever." Those two intuitions get combined, and you get this lumpy front with a long tail. Some of the tail probably comes from a minority of respondents who think certain things are just really hard, or who doubt current approaches will scale, and they push their mass way out.

I'd also be cautious about over-reading the precision. We've found big framing effects in these surveys. If you ask people for the probability of something happening by a given year, versus asking what year they'd give a given probability, you get noticeably different answers. And asking about automating all occupations versus achieving "high-level machine intelligence" gives wildly different timelines, even though they should be roughly the same thing. So the shape partly reflects real beliefs and partly reflects that people haven't thought carefully about these exact questions and are building answers on the spot.

So my overall take is that the near-term concentration is telling us something real: many researchers think a lot of these capabilities could come pretty soon, and that's worth taking seriously. The long tail tells us there's deep uncertainty and disagreement, and nobody should feel confident it'll take a very long time either. If anything, a distribution like that argues for preparing early, because even a modest chance of something transformative arriving in the next decade or two is a lot of probability to ignore.

r001.rationale: The response says arrival cannot precede today, while there is no natural endpoint afterward, linking that bounded-present/unbounded-future asymmetry to near-term probability and a long tail.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the thing that I find striking about this is that when you look at the aggregate distributions, people are putting a lot of probability on things happening fairly soon, like within the next decade or two, but then the distribution doesn't just end there. It kind of trails off, and a non-trivial amount of probability ends up on things taking fifty, a hundred, or more years, or in some cases essentially never.

I think there are a couple of things going on. One is that it's genuinely hard to know, and if you're uncertain in a sort of principled way, a long tail is the right shape. You can see fast progress right now and think it's quite likely to continue, but you also have to allow for the possibility that we hit some wall that we don't currently understand, and if we hit a wall, there's no particular reason it would take five years rather than fifty to get past it. So the tail is partly just honest ignorance about what the hard parts are.

The other thing is that I don't think these numbers come from a very unified model in most people's heads. When we ask researchers these questions, I suspect many of them are doing something like, "well, things are moving fast, so probably soon," and then separately, "but I've been wrong before, and people have been wrong before about AI, so let me hedge." And the hedging shows up as this long tail. It's not that they have a detailed story about why it would take eighty years. It's more a kind of generalized humility.

And I'd add that there's a real inconsistency you can find if you poke at it. If you ask about individual tasks, people tend to give shorter timelines than if you ask about automating all human occupations, even though those should be closely related. So I'd be cautious about reading the shape of the distribution as reflecting some deep, well-thought-out view. It's more like a mixture of "I can see the trend" and "I don't trust the trend," and both of those are showing up in the same curve.

That said, I don't think the near-term concentration should be dismissed just because the tail exists. Even if people are hedging, the fact that the median is as short as it is, and that it's been getting shorter in our surveys, is itself informative. If the people closest to the work think there's a decent chance of very capable systems soon, that's worth taking seriously, even if they're also unsure enough to leave a lot of mass further out.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the long tail to uncertainty about obstacles and generalized hedging. It does not suggest that the tail reflects the short interval up to the median versus the unlimited time available afterward.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s quite a natural shape for uncertainty to have. You might think there’s a reasonable chance that the approaches we already have will get us to a particular capability fairly soon. But if they don’t, it’s much less clear what’s missing or how long it will take to find it. So you can have quite a lot of probability in the next few years and still leave a long tail where it takes decades or longer.

It’s also useful to distinguish uncertainty within a researcher’s forecast from disagreement between researchers. If you’re looking at an aggregate, some of that tail could come from people who are much more pessimistic about progress. The shape alone doesn’t tell us how much is each. But I wouldn’t interpret a concentration in the near term as confidence that the task will definitely be achieved soon.

r001.rationale: The response explains the long tail through uncertainty about what is missing and how long it may take to find it, but does not connect the shape to the shorter time before a predicted median versus unlimited time afterward.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that pattern is consistent with people being quite uncertain about what’s required. You might think there’s a reasonable chance that the techniques we have are basically sufficient, and then a task could be achieved fairly soon. But if they aren’t sufficient, you don’t necessarily know what the missing piece is or how long it will take to find it. So you can have a lot of probability in the near term and still have a very long tail.

And if you’re combining forecasts from different researchers, that can also reflect disagreement. Some people expect things to happen soon; others think they’re much further away. The aggregate doesn’t necessarily describe any one person’s view.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the pattern to uncertainty about missing techniques and disagreement among researchers. It does not mention the asymmetry between the short wait to the predicted median and the unlimited time afterward.
